def: The Official Community Plan — the District's long-term rulebook for where homes, shops and parks can go. Council is due to rewrite it.
A floating hotel moored in Howe Sound to house Woodfibre LNG construction workers.
Homes rented or sold below the going rate, usually run by a non-profit rather than a landlord or developer.
Adding homes inside the existing town — on empty lots or by replacing one house with a few — instead of building on new land.
The line on the map beyond which the District has agreed not to spread. Building outside it means new roads, pipes and services.
Land that has never been built on before.
Starting each year's budget from nothing and justifying every dollar, instead of adjusting last year's numbers.
Money or land a developer gives the town in exchange for permission to build more — often put toward parks, daycares or trails.
Development cost charges — fees builders pay toward the water, sewer and road capacity their project will use.
Housing with staff and services on site for people who have been homeless or need daily help.
A provincial program that funds temporary housing to move people out of encampments.
The downtown Squamish building that houses the shelter and support services.
Changing the rules for a piece of land so something different can be built there. It needs a council vote.
Council's sign-off on how a specific building will look and sit on its lot.
Permission to break one of the town's own rules for a single project — for example, providing fewer parking spaces than required.
A Temporary Use Permit — short-term permission for a use the zoning wouldn't normally allow.
Someone already holding the seat who is running again.
A public-private partnership — the town teams up with a private company to build or run something.
The chief administrative officer — the District's top non-elected staff member, who runs day-to-day operations.
A B.C. law that forces towns to allow more homes on lots that used to be single-house only.
A number of new homes the Province orders a town to approve by a set date.
Land set aside for businesses and industry so the town has jobs, not only houses.
A group of tents or shelters where people without housing are living.
A ballot you request, fill in at home and return, instead of going to a voting place.
Voting on one of the earlier days set aside before election day. Anyone can use it; no reason needed.
The official word for a person who is allowed to vote.
Elected automatically because nobody ran against them.
